one_liner: Eager LINQ-style C# extension methods, with optional SIMD and parallel variants, for arrays, Span and List; beat .NET Framework LINQ 4-55x in 2017.
what_it_does: Provides LINQ-like extension methods (Sum, Min, Max, Average, Select, Where, OrderBy, Contains, SequenceEqual and others) on T[], Span<T> and List<T> that run immediately and return arrays or lists instead of lazy IEnumerable<T> pipelines. Method names carry a suffix so they sit alongside System.Linq: F for scalar, S for SIMD (arrays only), P for parallel and SP for SIMD plus parallel. Fused operations (WhereSelectF, SelectWhereF, WhereAggregateF) and in-place variants (SelectInPlaceF, ReverseInPlaceF) avoid intermediate allocations. It ships as four independent packages: LinqFaster, LinqFaster.SIMD, LinqFaster.Parallel and LinqFaster.SIMD.Parallel.
how_it_is_fast: The scalar methods index the array or list directly instead of going through IEnumerable<T> MoveNext/Current interface calls, and they allocate no enumerator. The S methods accumulate in System.Numerics.Vector<T> registers, whose width the JIT picks (8 ints with AVX2), and reduce horizontally at the end. Generic arithmetic is a chain of typeof(T) == typeof(int) tests that RyuJIT folds away for value types. OrderByF computes a key array and calls Array.Sort(keys, items), an unstable introsort, where LINQ OrderBy runs a stable, lazily enumerated sort. The P and SP methods split the array into ranges across Environment.ProcessorCount tasks.
when_to_use: Hot Sum, Min, Max or Average calls over primitive arrays in code pinned to .NET Framework 4.6.1+ or netstandard2.0, including Unity, which the base package targets.
Float or int array reductions where SIMD's reordered or unchecked arithmetic is acceptable: SumS ran 9.8 us against 541 us for LINQ on 100,000 ints in 2017.
Select-then-ToArray or Where-then-Aggregate patterns on arrays where the fused or in-place methods remove intermediate allocations.
Sorting arrays by a key when stability does not matter: OrderByF ran about 4.35x faster than LINQ OrderBy in the 2017 run.
Very large arrays or expensive per-element work for the P and SP methods; the README warns they allocate and may not beat the scalar or SIMD versions.
when_not_to_use: .NET 7 and later: runtime LINQ vectorized Min, Max, Sum and Average for arrays and lists in .NET 7, and Enumerable.Sum in .NET 8 (with overflow checks), per search snippets of a PVS-Studio article and a Microsoft compatibility notice. The README itself says that as of .NET 9 the library is 'mostly unnecessary'.

When you need LINQ's exact semantics: SumS, SumSP and AverageS on int wrap on overflow instead of throwing; OrderByF is not stable; and chained F calls are eager, so each step allocates and iterates where LINQ would make one lazy pass.
ContainsS on arrays whose length is a multiple of Vector<T>.Count: it misses matches in the last vector-width block (open issue #31; the bug is still in the code at HEAD).
Small integer element types with the SIMD sum: SumS on ushort[] throws InvalidCastException (open issue #18).
SIMD over List<T> or Span<T>: the S and SP methods exist only for arrays.

integration.dependencies: LinqFaster: System.Memory 4.5.3; LinqFaster.SIMD: System.Numerics.Vectors 4.5.0; LinqFaster.Parallel and LinqFaster.SIMD.Parallel: System.Threading.Tasks.Parallel 4.3.0 on netstandard1.3 (SIMD.Parallel also System.Numerics.Vectors 4.5.0)
integration.min_toolchain: netstandard2.0 or net461 for LinqFaster; netstandard2.0 for LinqFaster.SIMD; netstandard1.3, netstandard2.0 or net461 for the two parallel packages. SIMD gains need a JIT with hardware-accelerated Vector<T> (the benchmarks used 64-bit RyuJIT on .NET Framework 4.x).
integration.platforms: Any .NET runtime that supports those targets, Unity included for the base package; the SIMD width follows the JIT and CPU (SSE or AVX2).
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the methods are static and keep no shared state, and the P and SP methods use Tasks internally.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: names add an F, S, P or SP suffix; methods are eager and return arrays or lists; OrderByF is unstable; SIMD sums are unchecked

gotchas: ContainsS at HEAD loops while i < source.Length - count and then scans leftovers from Length - Length % count. When Length is a multiple of Vector<T>.Count, the last full vector is never checked, so new[]{1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8}.ContainsS(5) returns false. This is issue #31, open since April 2022 with a one-character fix proposed.

SumS(selectorSIMD) silently drops the leftover elements unless you also pass the scalar selector. It steps by Vector<U>.Count while loading Vector<T>, so it is only correct when T and U have the same width. SequenceCompareS reinterprets comparison masks as Vector<int>, so it is only correct for 32-bit element types.
SumF is checked, like LINQ Sum, but SumS and SumSP are not. AverageS sums through SumS, so int averages wrap on overflow, and float sums differ from the scalar results (the README notes this).

On nuget.org, LinqFaster stops at 1.0.0 (2018-02-05) while the repo's csproj is 1.1.0 with the Span<T> overloads added in February 2019. The Span support appears to be unpublished in the base package (other package IDs were not checked). LinqFaster.SIMD's last release is 1.0.3 (2019-07-12).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: LinqFaster is the only catalogued SIMD entry that offers generic LINQ-shaped reductions for C#. The other SIMD libraries are C, C++, Rust or Go (tphakala/simd, argminmax, sse-popcount), and Quickenshtein, the other .NET entry, only computes Levenshtein distance. Pick LinqFaster for legacy .NET Framework, netstandard2.0 or Unity code that wants SIMD Sum, Min, Max or Average over primitive arrays without writing Vector<T> loops; on modern .NET use the built-in LINQ.
verified_claims_summary: BenchmarkDotNet 0.10.3, .NET Framework 4.x 64-bit RyuJIT, Core i7-6600U, 100,000 random ints in [-100, 100) (Benchmarks.cs at commit f729004, 2017-03-31). LINQ Min took 548.9 us against 14.5 us for MinS (37.8x). LINQ Sum took 541.4 us against 9.76 us for SumS (55.4x), but SumS is unchecked; the like-for-like checked scalar SumF at 53.8 us is about 10x. OrderBy took 24,436 us against 5,613 us for the unstable OrderByF (4.35x). All ratios are derived from page data. The README's SumFastSIMDParallel row (3.7074 us) is not valid evidence (see status_note).
status_note: Harness flaw: the README's SumFastSIMDParallel row (3.7074 us, added in commit 5c5403e on 2017-03-31) was measured on SumPS. Its ForStrideAggregate lambdas captured the shared loop variable index, so tasks that started after the loop finished summed an empty range and the result was wrong. The capture was fixed the next day (11a5421, 'fixing parallel bugs'), after which the author committed 'parallel simd sum fixed but now is slow :D' (e8eb1d7), and the row was never re-measured. Separately, the library is stale: its code is unchanged since 2019-07-12 and the last commit (2025-09-26) only edited the README. It is MIT-licensed and small enough to copy, but obsolete on .NET 7 and later, and the ContainsS bug remains open.
